title: Two-dimensional nonces
stem: ERC-4337 EntryPoint nonces are two-dimensional: a 192-bit key and a 64-bit sequence. An account has executed exactly one UserOperation on key 1 and nothing else. What does EntryPoint.getNonce(account, 1) return, as a plain decimal integer?
mistake: "1": returns only the sequence and leaves out the key in the high 192 bits

title: personal_sign of a hex-looking string
stem: A dapp calls personal_sign (EIP-191 version 0x45) with the message given as the ten-character text string 0xdeadbeef. The wallet treats it as those ten UTF-8 characters, not as four bytes. Which exact preimage does the wallet keccak256-hash to get the 32-byte digest it signs?

options.A: "\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n4" followed by the four raw bytes 0xde 0xad 0xbe 0xef
options.B: "\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n8" followed by the eight ASCII characters "deadbeef"
options.C: "\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n10" followed by the ten ASCII characters "0xdeadbeef"
options.D: "\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n10" followed by the four raw bytes 0xde 0xad 0xbe 0xef

mistake: decoding the hex to 4 bytes with length 4

title: Reentrancy
stem: A Solidity withdraw function reads the caller's balance, sends that amount of ETH to the caller with a low-level call, and only sets the caller's balance to zero after the call returns. An attacker's contract uses its receive function to call withdraw again before the first call finishes, which drains the contract. What is the name of this vulnerability class?

options.A: Denial of service via unexpected revert
options.B: Reentrancy
options.C: Front-running
options.D: Unchecked call return value

mistake: Unchecked call return value (the low-level call looks like the bug)

title: Read-only reentrancy
stem: A liquidity pool lets users remove liquidity. During removal it sends ETH to the user with a low-level call and only afterwards updates its internal reserves. A separate lending protocol prices the pool's LP token by calling the pool's public view function `getVirtualPrice()`, which reads those reserves. The pool's own state-changing functions are all guarded with nonReentrant, and the pool is never drained. Yet the lending protocol is exploited. What happened?

options.A: During the ETH callback the pool's reserves were already reduced but the LP supply was not yet updated (or vice versa), so getVirtualPrice() returned a skewed value; the attacker called the lending protocol from inside the callback, and it priced the LP token on that stale state
options.B: The lending protocol's borrow() function had no nonReentrant modifier, so the attacker reentered borrow() over and over from an ETH callback and took out several loans against the same LP collateral before the protocol's debt accounting was written back to storage
options.C: The attacker reentered the pool's removeLiquidity through the ETH callback before reserves were updated and withdrew the same LP position twice; the inflated LP balance left behind was then posted as collateral in the lending protocol to borrow against funds that no longer existed
options.D: The pool's getVirtualPrice() view function was not marked payable, so when the lending protocol called it with ETH attached the call reverted silently inside a try/catch, and the protocol fell back to a hardcoded default LP price of 1e18 that the attacker could then borrow against

mistake: reentering removeLiquidity to withdraw twice

title: Cross-function reentrancy
stem: A contract tracks `balances[msg.sender]`. `withdraw()` is marked nonReentrant: it sends the caller's full balance with a low-level call, then zeroes the balance. `transfer(address to, uint256 amount)` has no modifier and simply moves balance between accounts. Can an attacker still profit, and how?

options.A: No: a low-level call forwards only a 2300-gas stipend to the recipient, so the attacker's fallback runs out of gas before it can make any call back into the contract
options.B: Yes: during withdraw()'s external call, before the balance is zeroed, the fallback calls transfer() to move the still-credited balance to a second account, which then withdraws it
options.C: No: nonReentrant on withdraw() sets a contract-wide lock that blocks every reentrant path into the contract, so the fallback's call to transfer() also reverts with a reentrancy error
options.D: Yes: the attacker calls withdraw() twice in one transaction from two different addresses, and the second call pays out its balance before the first call has zeroed the balance

mistake: believing nonReentrant on withdraw() protects transfer() too

title: Vault inflation attack
stem:
A USDC vault on Ethereum mainnet mints shares on deposit as `assets * totalShares / (USDC the vault currently holds)`; when share supply is zero, the first depositor gets one share per unit deposited. Redeeming burns shares and pays out the same pro-rata slice. This sequence happened:

  0xA1 deposit(1) (one unit, 0.000001 USDC) and receives 1 share, so share supply is 1.
  0xA1 does a plain ERC-20 transfer of 20,000 USDC straight to the vault address (not a call into the contract).
  0xB2 deposit(15,000 USDC). The transaction succeeds, and 0xB2 receives 0 shares.
  0xA1 redeems its 1 share and receives 35,000.000001 USDC.

No admin function ran, and the vault made no external calls other than the USDC transfers. The team must stay ERC-4626 compatible. Which change stops this attack for all future depositors?

options.A: Add a minimum-shares-out check to deposit() that reverts whenever the minted shares fall below the amount the depositor passes in as expected.
options.B: Add an owner-only sweep function that moves any USDC held above the tracked deposit total out of the vault to the treasury multisig.
options.C: Make the vault reject direct ERC-20 transfers, so that only a call to deposit() can ever raise the USDC balance it holds.
options.D: Add a virtual shares-and-assets offset to the conversion math (as OpenZeppelin's ERC4626 does) so deposits don't round to zero.

mistake: minimum-shares-out / slippage check as the fix

title: Spot price oracles
stem: Design review for a lending market on Ethereum mainnet. Positions hold up to $2M of WETH collateral backing USDC debt and are liquidated at 85% LTV. A teammate proposes pricing collateral by reading slot0 of the Uniswap V3 WETH/USDC 0.05% pool, which holds about $200M of liquidity. Their argument: moving that pool's price 10% would take tens of millions of dollars of trading, and arbitrage bots would pull the price back within the same block, so an attacker would lose money for nothing. What is the right assessment of this design?

options.A: Keep slot0, but add a circuit breaker that rejects any price more than 5% away from the previous block's stored price and pauses new borrows until it settles. That blocks a sudden 10% move while avoiding Chainlink's staleness risk and third-party dependency.
options.B: Reject it: a flash loan lets the attacker move the pool, borrow or liquidate against the bad price, and unwind in one transaction, so the cost is only fees plus slippage. Use a Chainlink feed and check the answer is positive and updatedAt is within its heartbeat.
options.C: Replace slot0 with a median of spot prices from the 0.05%, 0.3% and 1% WETH/USDC pools, read in the same call. One attacker cannot move all three pools at once without paying slippage on each, so the median stays within a fraction of a percent of the market price.
options.D: Accept it: at $200M of depth, a 10% move puts tens of millions of the attacker's own capital at risk, and same-block arbitrage makes the attack lose money. Add a check that the price is non-zero and inside the pool's valid tick range before using it.

mistake: accepting the pool-depth / arbitrage cost argument

title: Books that do not close
stem:
A single-token staking pool on Ethereum mainnet has been live for three weeks and its books do not close.

- 1,250,000 TKN has been staked in total since launch, and 250,000 TKN has been unstaked.
- The sum of stakedBalance[user] across all current stakers is 1,000,000 TKN.
- The pool contract's actual TKN balance is 975,000 TKN.
- Early unstakers were all paid. Users unstaking now are starting to revert with the token's insufficient-balance error.
- One user staked 10,000 TKN, and the UI showed 10,000 staked. When they unstaked all 10,000, their wallet received 9,800 TKN.

Here is the whole contract. stake(amount) calls token.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount), then sets stakedBalance[msg.sender] += amount. unstake(amount) decrements stakedBalance[msg.sender], then calls token.transfer(msg.sender, amount). There is no rewards logic and no admin withdrawal. The pool has never sent TKN anywhere except back to unstakers. TKN's total supply has not been changed and no rebase has occurred.

Which option correctly explains the missing 25,000 TKN and gives the right fix for stake()?

options.A: unstake() can be re-entered through a token callback, so some users withdrew twice. Fix: add a nonReentrant guard to unstake() and fund the gap from the treasury.
options.B: TKN is quietly rebasing downward, so the pool's balance shrinks over time. Fix: store each staker's share of the pool balance instead of raw token amounts.
options.C: TKN takes a 2% fee on every transfer, so the pool receives less than it credits. Fix: credit amount * 98 / 100 on stake so each recorded balance matches the tokens that arrived.
options.D: TKN takes about a 2% fee on every transfer, so the pool receives less than the amount it credits. Fix: credit token.balanceOf(pool) after transferFrom minus the balance before.

mistake: hardcoded 2% fee instead of measuring the balance change

title: OpenZeppelin v5 approvals

options.A: USDT reverts on approving a non-zero allowance over a non-zero one; use SafeERC20.forceApprove(token, strategy, amount), which zeroes it first when needed.
options.B: The leftover plus the new amount overflows USDT's allowance check; call token.increaseAllowance(strategy, amount - leftover) to top up the existing allowance instead of approving from scratch each run.
options.C: USDT's approve returns no bool, so the low-level call reports ok == false; decode the return data manually and treat an empty return payload as a successful approval before the require.
options.D: USDT reverts on approving a non-zero allowance over a non-zero one; use SafeERC20.safeApprove(token, strategy, amount), which handles the zero reset for you before approving.

mistake: safeApprove, which was removed in OZ v5

title: Signature replay
stem: A gasless order relayer contract verifies user-signed orders (owner, token, amount, nonce, deadline). It recovers the signer, checks the nonce is unused, checks the deadline, marks the nonce used, and moves tokens. The digest is keccak256(abi.encodePacked("\x19\x01", DOMAIN_SEPARATOR, structHash)), where DOMAIN_SEPARATOR is computed once in the constructor from the contract name, a version string and address(this), and stored in an immutable. The same contract is deployed with CREATE2 (same factory and salt) at an identical address on Ethereum mainnet, Base and Arbitrum. A user signed one 5,000 USDC order, and it executed on Base. Minutes later someone submitted the same signature to the mainnet deployment, and it passed every check there too. The team wants to keep the same address on every chain. What is the root cause, and what is the right fix?

options.A: The domain separator omits chainId, so the digest is the same on every chain. Add chainId to the EIP-712 domain, and rebuild the separator whenever block.chainid differs from the cached value.
options.B: The per-user nonce is meant to stop replays, so the mainnet deployment must have skipped the nonce check before marking it used. Fix the nonce bookkeeping so a nonce consumed on any deployment is rejected on every other one.
options.C: The shared CREATE2 address makes the verifyingContract field identical on all three chains, so the domain separators collide. Deploy with a different salt per chain so each address, and so each domain separator, is unique.
options.D: Signature malleability let the attacker submit a flipped-s copy of the Base signature, which ecrecover still maps to the same owner. Enforce low-s values and reject v values other than 27 or 28 when recovering the signer.

mistake: blaming the nonce check (nonces are per-deployment)

title: The upgrade that succeeded
stem:
A staking protocol uses a UUPS-upgradeable contract on Ethereum mainnet. V1 declared its state in this order:

  uint256 public totalDeposited;  // held 2_000_000_000000 (2,000,000 USDC)
  address public treasury;        // held 0xC0FFEE0000000000000000000000000000000000
  uint256 public feeBps;          // held 500

The team upgraded to V2, which declares, in order:

  uint256 public rewardIndex;     // new in V2
  uint256 public totalDeposited;
  address public treasury;
  uint256 public feeBps;

There is no re-initializer, and the upgrade did not rewrite any existing value. The upgrade transaction succeeded, the proxy points at the V2 they deployed, the proxy admin is unchanged, and no call reverts. After the upgrade, the proxy returns:

  rewardIndex()    -> 2000000000000 (never set)
  totalDeposited() -> a huge number that, in hex, is exactly the old treasury address
  treasury()       -> 0x00000000000000000000000000000000000001F4
  feeBps()         -> 0

They still need rewardIndex in V2. Which diagnosis and fix is correct?

options.A: Putting rewardIndex first moved every variable down one slot. The V1 values are still in slots 0–2. Ship a corrected V2 that declares rewardIndex after feeBps.
options.B: V2's new variables were never initialized because there is no re-initializer. Add a reinitializer(2) that copies V1's values into totalDeposited, treasury and feeBps.
options.C: The upgrade overwrote V1's storage with V2's layout, so the deposit data is lost. Deploy a fresh proxy with rewardIndex appended and rebuild balances from event logs.
options.D: V2's slot 0 collides with the proxy's implementation pointer because EIP-1967 slots were not used. Move the implementation address to the EIP-1967 slot and redeploy V2.

mistake: missing re-initializer diagnosis

title: Checks, effects, interactions
stem: A Solidity function body is ordered so that it first validates inputs and conditions, then updates all contract state, and only performs external calls last. What is the standard name of this defensive coding pattern?

options.A: Pull-over-Push (withdrawal pattern)
options.B: Reentrancy Guard (nonReentrant mutex)
options.C: Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI)
options.D: Validate-Execute-Commit (VEC) ordering

mistake: Reentrancy Guard, the related defense mistaken for the ordering pattern

title: Missing access control
stem: A deployed contract that holds user funds has a function `emergencyWithdraw()` marked `external` with no modifiers. Its body sends the contract's entire token balance to `msg.sender`. Anyone who calls it gets all the funds. What vulnerability class is this?

options.A: Missing access control (an unprotected privileged function)
options.B: Unchecked return value (the token transfer result is ignored)
options.C: Front-running (the withdraw call can be sandwiched in the mempool)
options.D: Reentrancy (state not updated before the external transfer)

mistake: reentrancy, the usual label given to any withdraw drain

title: Upgrade storage layout
stem: A contract behind an upgradeable proxy declared, in V1, exactly two storage variables in this order: `uint256 a; uint256 b;`. You are writing V2 and need to add a new variable `uint256 c`. Which V2 storage layout is safe?

options.A: Any order is safe because variable names are preserved across upgrades
options.B: uint256 c; uint256 a; uint256 b;
options.C: uint256 a; uint256 c; uint256 b;
options.D: uint256 a; uint256 b; uint256 c;

mistake: any order safe because names are preserved

title: UUPS authorization
stem: You are writing an upgradeable implementation contract that inherits OpenZeppelin's UUPSUpgradeable. There is one internal function you must override (typically restricted with an owner check such as onlyOwner) to control who may perform upgrades; getting it wrong can leave the contract locked or open to anyone. Which function is it?

options.A: proxiableUUID()
options.B: _upgradeTo(address newImplementation)
options.C: upgradeToAndCall(address newImplementation, bytes data)
options.D: _authorizeUpgrade(address newImplementation)

mistake: upgradeToAndCall: the public entry point, not the auth hook

title: Sandwiches and slippage
stem: You submit a swap of 10 ETH for USDC on Uniswap through the public mempool with a 1% slippage tolerance. A bot sees your pending transaction, buys USDC immediately before yours executes (pushing the price up), lets your swap fill at the worse price, then sells immediately after your transaction, pocketing the difference. What is this specific MEV attack called?

options.A: A sandwich attack
options.B: A just-in-time (JIT) liquidity attack
options.C: A frontrunning attack
options.D: A backrunning attack

mistake: frontrunning (names only one leg)

title: Lending post-mortem: the sequencer

options.A: Read the Chainlink L2 Sequencer Uptime Feed. While it reports down and for an hour after it comes back, pause the whole market: deposits, top-ups, repayments and liquidations all revert.
options.B: Tighten the staleness bound from 3600 seconds to about 300 seconds, and add an answeredInRound >= roundId check so a stale or carried-over round can never be used to price a liquidation.
options.C: Read the Chainlink L2 Sequencer Uptime Feed and revert every price read, for every action, while it reports the sequencer down. Liquidations resume in the first block after the feed reports it back up.
options.D: Read the Chainlink L2 Sequencer Uptime Feed. Block liquidations while it reports down and for about an hour after it returns; keep deposits, top-ups and repayments open.

mistake: tightening the staleness bound (also: no grace period)

title: Lending post-mortem: the clock

options.A: Like Arbitrum, Base's block.number returns the L1 block number read from its L1Block predeploy, so 12 s per block holds on Base too and it will also charge about 3,391 USDC.
options.B: Arbitrum's block.number returns an approximate L1 block number, so 12 s fits. Base's block.number counts 2 s L2 blocks, so it charges about 6x: roughly 20,400 USDC.
options.C: Arbitrum's block.number counts L2 blocks, but its sequencer only makes blocks when transactions arrive, so they average near 12 s. Base's steady 2 s blocks will charge about 6x.
options.D: Arbitrum's block.number returns an approximate L1 block number, so 12 s fits. Base's block.number counts 2 s L2 blocks, so it under-charges by 6x: roughly 566 USDC for July.

mistake: assuming Base's block.number tracks L1 like Arbitrum's

title: Lending post-mortem: the signature

options.A: Signature replay: the signed struct has no nonce or expiry, and nothing records used signatures. Fix: add a nonce and a deadline to the Borrow typehash and struct, check the deadline, and increment the signer's nonce on use.
options.B: Signature malleability: ecrecover accepts high-s values, so anyone can swap s for secp256k1n - s and flip v between 27 and 28 to get a second valid signature. Fix: reject s above secp256k1n/2 and require v to be 27 or 28, as OpenZeppelin's ECDSA library does.
options.C: Signature replay: nothing stops reuse. Fix: keep a per-borrower nonce mapping in storage, require the stored nonce to be unused, and increment it on each borrowWithSig call, leaving the Borrow typehash and signed struct as they are so existing signatures stay valid.
options.D: Unauthenticated relayer: anyone can call borrowWithSig with a valid signature, and the June call came from an unknown address. Fix: restrict borrowWithSig to an allowlisted relayer address with an onlyRelayer modifier, and add a check that ecrecover does not return address(0).

mistake: blaming signature malleability (option 1); the on-chain nonce that is not signed over is also a targeted mistake

title: Decimal scale mismatch
stem: A lending market takes WETH (18 decimals) as collateral and lends USDC (6 decimals). It values collateral as `collateralWei * ethUsdPrice / 1e18`, giving a USD value with 18 decimals, and it allows a borrow when `debtRaw <= collateralValue * 70 / 100`, where `debtRaw` is the raw USDC amount the borrower is requesting. By what factor does this check overstate how much USDC a borrower may take, compared to a correct check?
mistake: 1000000: taking USDC's 6 decimals as the gap, not 18 − 6 = 12

title: Permissionless token listing

options.A: Measure the vault's token balance before and after the transfer, and mint shares on the amount actually received.
options.B: Nothing extra: SafeERC20's safeTransferFrom already reverts whenever the vault receives less than the requested amount.
options.C: Add OpenZeppelin's nonReentrant guard to deposit and withdraw so a token callback can't change the share math mid-call.
options.D: State in NOTES.md that fee-on-transfer tokens are unsupported, and ask operators to avoid ever listing such tokens.

mistake: trusting SafeERC20 to catch fee-on-transfer shortfalls

title: Build a borrowing market
stem: You are building a small borrowing market on Ethereum mainnet. Users lock WETH as collateral and borrow USDC against it, up to 70% of the collateral's value. If a position's debt goes above 85% of its collateral value, anyone can repay part of the debt and take the matching WETH plus a 5% bonus. The contract has to price WETH in USD to check health and liquidations. Which price source should it use?

options.A: The live spot price of the deepest Uniswap V3 WETH/USDC pool, read from slot0's sqrtPriceX96 and converted to a USDC-per-WETH price
options.B: A Chainlink ETH/USD feed read via latestAnswer(), scaled from 8 to 18 decimals and used directly as the WETH price with no further checks
options.C: A Chainlink ETH/USD feed read via latestRoundData(), rejecting answers that are stale (updatedAt older than the heartbeat) or not positive
options.D: The reserve ratio of the Uniswap V2 WETH/USDC pair from getReserves(), since arbitrage keeps that deep mainnet pool close to the market price

mistake: Reading the spot price from Uniswap V3 slot0 (can be manipulated in one transaction)

title: A permit request

options.A: It is a USDC permit giving 0x1661…3Ee3 an allowance of about 1,033,366 USDC. The allowance stays live until the deadline, so the spender could submit permit() today and then transferFrom() the full amount right away. Don't sign.
options.B: It is a USDC permit giving 0x1661…3Ee3 an allowance of about 1,033,366 USDC. The deadline (2023-03-13) has passed, so this copy would fail today, but an unknown spender asking for it is hostile. Don't sign.
options.C: It is a USDC permit giving 0x1661…3Ee3 an allowance of about 1,033,366 USDC. The deadline (2023-03-13) has already passed, so permit() will always revert with an expired-deadline error and the signature is useless to anyone. It is harmless and safe to sign.
options.D: It is a USDC permit giving 0x1661…3Ee3 an allowance of about 0.000001 USDC (value read with 18 decimals, as for most ERC-20 tokens). That is a tiny dust amount, so even an unknown spender can't take anything real from the account. It is safe to sign.

mistake: calling it safe to sign because the deadline has expired

title: A Permit2 batch

options.A: It is the routine Uniswap Permit2 approval. Permit2 at 0x000000000022D473030F116dDEE9F6B43aC78BA3 is Uniswap's own contract, so the allowance can only be spent through Uniswap's router for swaps the user starts. Safe to sign.
options.B: It gives 0x1661…3Ee3 unlimited (max uint160) USDC, WETH and DAI allowances until March 2030. The tokens are already approved to Permit2, so the spender can submit this signature and pull funds with no further user action. Don't sign.
options.C: It is only an off-chain signature. No tokens can move until the user sends a separate on-chain approve transaction for each of USDC, WETH and DAI naming 0x1661…3Ee3 as spender, so it is safe to sign and ignore.
options.D: It is a one-time transfer permit. Nonce 0 is used up on first use, so the spender can pull each of USDC, WETH and DAI only once before sigDeadline 1900000000 (March 2030). The risk is limited to one transfer per token.

mistake: thinking an off-chain signature can't move funds

title: A decimal is still an address
stem: A dapp sends eth_signTypedData_v4 whose domain contains "verifyingContract": 917551056842671309452305380979543736893630245704, a JSON number and not a hex string. The wallet's security checks compare the domain against a list of known token contracts. Which contract's domain is this?

options.A: USDC, 0xA0b86991c6218b36c1d19D4a2e9Eb0cE3606eB48
options.B: None; a decimal number matches no address in the list

mistake: not normalizing the decimal, so it matches nothing

title: Sign-in domain binding
stem:
A wallet receives a personal_sign request from the origin https://opensea-rewards.xyz. The message is:

opensea.io wants you to sign in with your Ethereum account:
0xd8dA6BF26964aF9D7eEd9e03E53415D37aA96045

URI: https://opensea.io
Version: 1
Chain ID: 1
Nonce: 8f3c1a9b
Issued At: 2026-09-21T10:00:00Z

What should the wallet do?

options.A: Sign after checking that the nonce 8f3c1a9b has not been used before and that Issued At 2026-09-21T10:00:00Z is recent, since a fresh, unused nonce prevents replay and is what makes a Sign-In with Ethereum message safe
options.B: Sign: personal_sign only produces an EIP-191 signature over text, so it cannot move funds, approve tokens or grant allowances, which means a sign-in message carries no risk and there is nothing here for the wallet to protect
options.C: Refuse or warn loudly: in Sign-In with Ethereum the message domain must match the requesting origin; a mismatch means this site is collecting a signature that logs the user in to opensea.io
options.D: Sign: the message names opensea.io with URI https://opensea.io on Chain ID 1, and OpenSea is a legitimate, well-known marketplace, so the sign-in request can be trusted as coming from OpenSea itself

mistake: trusting the domain named in the message

title: Operation 1
stem: A Safe multisig transaction is waiting for your signature. The other owners have signed. Fields: to = 0x40A2aCCbd92BCA938b02010E17A5b8929b49130D (a MultiSend contract), value = 0, operation = 1, data = multiSend(...) whose decoded contents are a routine ERC-20 transfer to a known address. What does operation = 1 mean, and why is it the first field to check?

options.A: 1 means DELEGATECALL: the target's code runs with the Safe's own storage and address, so a malicious target can overwrite the singleton (mastercopy) slot and take over the Safe, whatever the decoded inner calls show; this is how the Bybit Safe was drained
options.B: 1 means "batch": it only tells the Safe that several calls are packed into the data field, so once the decoded inner calls look routine (here one ERC-20 transfer to a known address) there is nothing more to check and the transaction is safe to sign
options.C: 1 means CALL with value: it only matters when ETH is attached, so with value = 0 the flag has no effect, and the risk lies entirely in the decoded inner calls, which here are a routine ERC-20 transfer to a known address that the owners already recognize
options.D: operation is informational: the Safe records it in the SafeTx hash for off-chain tooling but ignores it when executing, always making a normal CALL to the target, so only the decoded contents of the data field decide what the transaction does

mistake: treating operation 1 as a harmless batch flag
